title: Four parts
hook: to Sigala: one part to live on, two for work, one kept for hard times (DN 31)
carry: enjoy some, build with some, protect some

segments.voice: Yesterday: anavajja-sukha, and your line, blameless is best. Which of the four did you find a trace of in your own life? Day three hundred eighty.

Early morning near Rajagaha. A young man named Sigala stands with his clothes and hair still wet, bowing in six directions: east, south, west, north, down, and up. His dying father told him to do this, and he does it faithfully, without knowing why. The Buddha, walking into town for alms, stops and asks what he's doing. Then, gently, he reinterprets the whole ritual. The six directions, he says, are the people in your life. What follows is a whole sutta of advice for ordinary life, and somewhere in the middle of it, there's a budget. Today: four parts.
screen: `WET HAIR, SIX BOWS.` → `HIS FATHER'S LAST WISH.` → `THE BUDDHA STOPS TO ASK.`

segments.voice: The six directions become six relationships. East is your parents. South, your teachers. West, your spouse and children. North, your friends. Below, those who work for you. Above, spiritual teachers. For each, the Buddha lists what you owe them and what they owe you. Then, in a run of verses, he turns to money. The wise person, he says, gathers wealth the way a bee gathers nectar, a little at a time, and it grows the way an anthill grows. Then the budget. Divide your wealth into four parts. Live on one part and enjoy it. Put two parts to work in your business. Keep the fourth part saved against hard times. One for living, two for work, one for the rainy day. It's ancient advice, and it would still make sense on a spreadsheet. Notice what it assumes: that a householder will have money, should enjoy some of it, should invest in their livelihood, and should plan for misfortune. Nothing here is otherworldly. The fractions don't map neatly onto a modern paycheck, and the tradition doesn't treat them as law. Some read the two parts for work as money invested, others as the costs of running a trade. But the shape is the lesson: enjoy some, build with some, protect some, and decide on purpose. The commentary on this sutta, traditionally credited to Buddhaghosa, calls it the discipline of the householder. Monks have their rules. This is a lay person's.
screen: `SIX DIRECTIONS, SIX RELATIONSHIPS.` · `LIKE A BEE, LIKE AN ANTHILL.` · `ONE TO LIVE, TWO TO WORK, ONE TO KEEP.` · `THE HOUSEHOLDER'S DISCIPLINE.` · then, large: `FOUR PARTS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Without opening any app, picture your money in four piles, roughly as it is right now. How big is the part you live on? The part that builds something: your work, your skills, your future? The part kept for hard times? Don't calculate. Just notice the shape, and how it feels in the body to look at it. Then rest, and let one small adjustment suggest itself, if one does. The bell holds the time.
Four parts. The Buddha's advice to Sigala: one part to live on, two for work, and one kept for hard times.
Your line: enjoy some, build with some, protect some. Today, look at one line of your budget and ask which of the four parts it belongs to. Day three hundred eighty.

howItsDone: The Sigalovada Sutta is widely taught to lay Buddhists, especially in Theravada countries, as practical guidance for family, friendship, work and money.

fork.setup: you're Sigala, still wet from bathing, bowing to six directions. the Buddha asks what you're doing. what does he do next?
options: tells you to stop the ritual.
reinterprets the six directions as your relationships.
fork.reveal: in DN 31 he doesn't scold the ritual; he turns the six directions into parents, teachers, family, friends, workers and spiritual teachers.

original.note: Pali bhoga: wealth, possessions. DN 31's verse tells the householder to divide his wealth in four.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha didn't care about money.
what it means: he gave a householder a budget: live on one part, work with two, keep one.
what a scholar hears: the four-part rule comes in DN 31's verses (catudhā vibhaje bhoge), and the commentary credited to Buddhaghosa calls the sutta gihi-vinaya, the householder's discipline.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: cut the uncited age ('two and a half thousand years old'); attributed 'the householder's discipline' to the commentary traditionally credited to Buddhaghosa and dropped 'great'.
DN 31 paraphrased. Rhys Davids's translation (Dialogues of the Buddha III, 1921) exists but was not quoted because its exact wording could not be confirmed.
Setting: the sutta places Sigala near Rajagaha, bowing with wet clothes and hair; confirm.
Six directions mapping: east parents, south teachers, west wife and children, north friends, nadir servants/workers, zenith ascetics and brahmins. Script says 'spiritual teachers' for the last.
Bee and anthill simile and the four-part verse (catudhā vibhaje bhoge) given from memory.
Buddhaghosa's description of DN 31 as gihi-vinaya: confirm.
